expected.outcome: mixed: one shape each up 12–25%, others down 10–45%
expected.why: the leaf cost is the insertion fix-up (Devroye's n·∫f²) and the per-bucket probes, not the counters or the level count; lever is equi-depth classes gated by an ∫f² estimate, branchless fix-up, fewer probes

expected.outcome: −5 to −28% at 14T, −10 to −16% at 6T on every random shape
expected.why: the scalar flash/coarse leaf on an L2-resident bucket is already ~9 ns/elem; the vectorized quicksort is 8.5 at 1 thread and slower under 14, on a hybrid P+E CPU (E-cores run 256-bit AVX2 double-pumped). The same code wins 1.2–1.6× sequentially, so it ships sequential-only

expected.outcome: 0.93–1.09× at 14T over two runs, 0.97–1.03× at 7T: noise
expected.why: the histogram's residual cost on bimodal is branch behaviour on alternating modes, not the child-table dereference the model removes; a model with worst error ≥2 buckets loops and cost −12% on heavy_tail even as a trial chunk
32 vectors spill; one more partition level (0.4–0.7 ns/elem) plus the 64 network is cheaper

expected.outcome: lognormal 0.91×, exponential 0.80× against the key splitter table it displaces
expected.why: a heavy tail decays *inside* each binade too, so its buckets take up to 3× their share and spill where the table's do not; the trial picks it anyway because it times the lookup, not the partition (which is what D37 now catches). First cut was worse still: indexed on the key's top byte, which holds 7 of the 11 exponent bits, so Pareto fell into two entries and 63% spilled

expected.outcome: 98.5% crossing mass on a staircase built with 10%
expected.why: a strand's last element lands at the head of the next interval and turns the neighbour's whole middle into a two-strand crossing; a first value cuts below itself, a last value above. Caught by the trace build before anything was timed

expected.outcome: 0.92–0.96 on the shapes just past the gate; the predicted break-even does not exist on the two-strand ladder
expected.why: see B58. Shipped gates are measured: 1.0n parallel (the pure-partition control), 3.0n sequential, 1.0n sequential with at most MERGE_MAX_RUNS runs

expected.outcome: 0.84–0.99 at 1M and 14 threads on rows that win at 8.4M
expected.why: the cap was measured on copies, which are bandwidth-bound; merges are compute-bound and ran on 2 threads against the partition's 10. The cap now counts work, n + 3 × cost: 1.26–1.43

expected.outcome: 0.89 against the pure partition at 14 threads, 2.4× at one
expected.why: staged copy plus an in-place merge tournament; declined early instead, the row rose from 1.16 to 1.24 against the shipped engine. A direct 3- or 4-way merge from the source is the untried angle

expected.outcome: three sorted elements 6 → 42 ns; random n = 32 781 → 2431 ns; block_perm n = 100 2105 → 4969 ns
expected.why: two getenv calls are ~40 ns; and when runs hold two or three elements nearly every element is a run endpoint, so almost nothing "crosses", the gate says go, and the sweep sorts the array the slow way. parse to a numeric key + logos_argsort_f64 + one gather is 8.48x over std::sort on std::string and 4.87x over fixed 24-byte memcmp records, 2M records, one thread. A format is worth what it saves in COMPARISON WIDTH, not in distribution knowledge

22.2% of 2.0M pairs at different indices come back order-INVERTED. proj_x = R*x/sqrt(x^2+p^2+z^2), and with z to 8.4M against values to 1e4 the z^2 term dwarfs x^2, so it orders by value/index. Cost alone would NOT have killed it: 2.89 ns/element against the engine's 0.60 ns addressing multiply-add
